title: Paradev workflows — presentation content
content:
Working material for the next talk: the original Mastra framework, our current Paradev workflows, and a practical path for someone starting with one recurring task. This is content development; visual production will use the Graphics project. Research snapshot: . The source appendix preserves the retrieved notes. Roadmap goals and reported case-study results are identified separately from product behavior we checked. ## The argument Start with a piece of work you already understand. Make the result inspectable. Save what makes the run work. Automate when it starts. Improve the constraint that now limits completed work. Someone should leave this talk able to set up one useful loop. They should also understand why launching more coding agents can make their day worse if review and decisions remain the bottleneck. ## 1. What the previous Mastra talk established [Original recording, post and transcript: How to run 100 agents in parallel and keep your sanity](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kiet-ho_i-had-the-honor-of-presenting-at-mastras-activity-7449892006153179137-3ivj) The previous talk maps development as Trigger → Plan → Code → Review → Merge. It uses merged PRs as an observable proxy for delivered value, asks which stage constrains throughput, and argues for increasing capacity where it helps the whole line. It covers event-triggered work, planning context, parallel environments, tests and visual validation. Human intent and architectural judgment remain review boundaries. The new talk can move from this framework to a practical question: how does one engineer start building that process, and how does a product help it improve? ## 2. Your own product thesis Kiet’s Q3 Product Roadmap is the clearest historical statement of the approach: build the building blocks for users to construct their factory, and use our own team as the first users. It names four primitives: - **Triggers:** what starts work and moves it to the next stage. - **Workspaces:** somewhere an agent and a person can execute, inspect and verify work. - **Memory:** the instructions and knowledge that connect stages and improve later runs. - **Visibility:** the metrics and evidence needed to tune the process. Homework (Kiet) 1 develops the learning side: users should not have to keep asking agents to save lessons, and knowledge should carry across agents and teammates. It proposes increasing merge rate while holding human effort per PR constant or reducing it. These are strategy statements and desired outcomes. They are not evidence of a measured productivity multiplier. ## 3. What this looks like inside Paradev ### The Home: a review request becomes an investigation The live Cloud PR review configuration we inspected starts a cloud agent on selected assignment, review-request and PR-opened events. Its instructions require checking the PR head, reading the surrounding code and discussion, inspecting CI, and trying the surfaces affected by the change. The result is a report with findings, test notes, screenshots or command output, and explicit gaps. It is linked from GitHub and Slack. The workflow then sleeps; another automation handles review-workspace cleanup on merge or close. The useful pattern for others is a request that produces evidence a human can inspect. The full Home setup is a mature example; a beginner can start with a local report on one PR. Sources: live Cloud PR review automation and prompt inspected during this session; [example review comment](https://github.com/ParadevAI/Paradev/pull/9675#issuecomment-6830979122). ### Coda and Martin: customer context travels with the work Martin reports that an iOS photo upload hangs. Coda matches the report to an existing issue, opens an investigation session after a human request, and returns a root cause, a proposed fix and an evidence link. The Home reviews the PR; the result goes to Harshith for the merge decision. [Customer thread](https://paradev-ai.slack.com/archives/C0CEJPMM39N/p1794501902030769) · [Coda’s follow-up](https://paradev-ai.slack.com/archives/C0CEJPMM39N/p1794505156233979) · [PR #9675](https://github.com/ParadevAI/Paradev/pull/9675) The important limit: the reviewer reported tests and simulator evidence for the cloud path, but could not exercise the affected host-workspace path in the app. A positive review still left a specific verification task for a person with that environment. The PR was open and unmerged when checked. ### Humans still decide scope In another Martin thread, a tooltip fix expands into a multi-PR feature request. Satya asks Coda to split that feature into a separate ticket. Coda does so, keeping the existing PR scoped. [Scope correction](https://paradev-ai.slack.com/archives/C0CEJPMM39N/p1794329071904259) · [PR #9594](https://github.com/ParadevAI/Paradev/pull/9594) This is a useful operating example: delegation does not remove product decisions. The PR was also open and unmerged when checked. ### Dev doctor: recurring repair should become code The configured Dev doctor process gathers failures, groups them by cause, checks existing tickets and maintains a notebook. Its instructions say that the same repair a third time should become a code fix or reconciler rule. An enabled hourly incident automation was inspected. We have not audited its history to demonstrate that it has reduced failures. Present it as a configured learning process. [Dev doctor instructions](https://github.com/ParadevAI/Paradev/blob/e5bac946514183a63bc95a7f47ad3193f5a19e3b/.agents/skills/dev-doctor/SKILL.md) ## 4. Start small: one recurring task ### Step 1 — Choose the task by the bottleneck Ask: what do I keep doing, what delays useful work, and what could an agent prepare for me? A first task should have accessible inputs, a clear boundary and an output the owner can check quickly. Examples: | Where work waits | Small first task | Result to inspect | | --- | --- | --- | | Reviewing PRs | Review one PR you select | Concrete findings with evidence and test gaps | | Investigating reports | Triage one selected bug | Reproduction, likely cause, or missing information | | Understanding CI | Explain one failed run | Failed check, relevant logs and recommended next step | | Writing release notes | Draft notes from selected merged PRs | A draft linked to its source changes | Pick the one that relieves your constraint. A team already drowning in open PRs may get more value from review assistance than an agent that produces another batch of patches. ### Step 2 — Run it manually Give the agent a real example and watch where you intervene. Does it lack credentials, choose the wrong repository, miss a rule, or return something hard to evaluate? Treat these interventions as information about what the workflow needs. Resolve the missing context before adding a schedule. A useful first result is narrow: an investigation report on one bug, not responsibility for every message in the customer channel. ### Step 3 — Define a result worth receiving Write down the input, the work to perform, the evidence required, the stopping condition and the person receiving it. For bug triage, the result could be: - The source report and the commit investigated. - What the agent reproduced and how. - Relevant code and evidence for the proposed explanation. - What it could not check. - One next action for the owner. “Done” should mean someone can make the next decision. A long transcript that requires another investigation has not saved much attention. ### Step 4 — Save the repeatable instructions Put stable process rules in a skill or document and pass the changing input separately. Keep a successful example alongside the instructions. Future runs should not depend on remembering the original chat. For a simple loop, a prompt, one instruction file and a report are enough. Add more elaborate memory when there is a recurring retrieval problem to solve. ### Step 5 — Add an opt-in trigger Once the manual run is useful, automate the handoff that starts it. An explicit review request, issue assignment or Slack reaction lets someone choose when the agent acts. For a Slack workflow in Paradev: 1. Pick the project, agent and local or cloud target under Automations. 2. Add a Slack Reaction added trigger, scoped to one channel and a chosen emoji. 3. Use a triage prompt that returns evidence and a recommendation. 4. Add the reaction to a real report. 5. Open the resulting workspace and assess the output before widening the trigger. This path is based on the documented recipe, not an automation created for this talk. A local target needs to stay online; use a suitable cloud environment when work must run without the laptop. [Slack bug-report recipe](https://github.com/ParadevAI/Paradev/blob/e5bac946514183a63bc95a7f47ad3193f5a19e3b/apps/docs/content/docs/recipes/slack-bug-reports.mdx) ### Step 6 — Add an action after the preparation works If investigations consistently produce useful evidence, allow a reproducible bug to become a proposed patch and draft PR. Keep the same owner and evidence requirements. If review becomes the new bottleneck, invest in review quality and environment access before increasing investigation volume. Expand along the work rather than turning on every trigger at once. ## 5. A starter prompt The following is a proposed first-run template. It prepares a report for human inspection and does not require a multi-agent system. ```text Investigate the bug report supplied with this run in this repository. Read the project instructions. Find the relevant code. Check whether an issue or PR already covers the report. Try to reproduce the behavior using the smallest relevant check. Use the running app if that is necessary to establish what happens. Write triage.html with: - the source report and commit investigated; - what you checked and the evidence; - what you reproduced, or the information still missing; - the relevant code locations; - one recommended next action. Do not change code, post messages, open tickets or create a PR. If you cannot establish the cause, record what you ruled out. Finish with the report path so I can inspect it. ``` For an unattended version, choose a durable destination for the report and an explicit delivery method. If that involves publishing a page or posting to a service, authorize that action in the workflow. A local file works for the supervised first run. A later version can permit a draft PR after reproduction. That is a deliberate expansion of the workflow. ## 6. Add reliability as soon as the run is unattended The first automation needs to cope with missing inputs and repeated events. - **Identify the work.** Use an issue ID, PR plus head commit, or another stable key. Check for an existing result before creating another. Where duplicate effects matter, enforce uniqueness in code; a prompt check alone can race. - **Make gaps visible.** Missing access or an unavailable app environment should produce a blocked result with a clear next action. - **Stop event loops.** An agent’s output should not repeatedly trigger the same work. Use narrow event scopes and actor filters where supported. - **Set a work budget.** Include a stopping condition and limit active runs to what the owner can inspect. Use enforced runtime or spend controls where available. - **Separate dispatch from completion.** Check the work product, not only whether a workspace started. Paradev’s documentation specifies at-least-once dispatch. Raw webhooks have no deduplication, and an accepted webhook may start zero runs. Current automation run history treats workspace creation as its success state; it does not establish successful task completion. [Automation contract](https://github.com/ParadevAI/Paradev/blob/e5bac946514183a63bc95a7f47ad3193f5a19e3b/apps/docs/content/docs/automations.mdx) ## 7. Webhooks are the next step when the signal comes from your own tools Prefer the existing trigger when it already expresses the event. A webhook is useful when an internal script, deploy system or other service needs to pass structured context. For example: send the service, commit and log URL for a failed deploy. The agent investigates and returns a report or proposed fix. This is an illustrative extension, not a verified internal deployment workflow. Start by sending one known payload and inspecting the result. Then decide which events should call it, how repeated deliveries are handled, and where completion is reported. [Webhook recipe](https://github.com/ParadevAI/Paradev/blob/e5bac946514183a63bc95a7f47ad3193f5a19e3b/apps/docs/content/docs/recipes/webhook-runs.mdx) ## 8. Make each useful run improve the next Keep a small record of what needed correction: | Observation | Durable response | | --- | --- | | The agent asks for the same project fact | Add it to the task instructions | | The same real defect recurs | Add a focused regression check | | The same manual recovery repeats | Propose a recovery rule in code | | Reports repeat a false finding | Add the counterexample to review guidance | | Work stalls awaiting a decision | Clarify ownership and surface that decision | Version changes to prompts, skills and recovery code. Review them and compare later results against examples that previously failed. One correction is evidence for a proposed improvement; it does not establish a universal rule. This is a concrete form of self-improvement: the operating process learns. It does not require a claim that the underlying model is training itself. ## 9. What to measure before scaling A simple run log can record the input, result, owner correction, human time spent, cost where available, and final outcome. Ask: - Did it produce something useful? - Did the owner spend less effort than doing the task directly? - Did it move completed work through the bottleneck? - Did it add rework or increase the queue downstream? - Did the same failure happen again after the process changed? For code-writing loops, follow a proposed fix through review, merge and actual use. A merged PR is a convenient proxy, but production behavior and customer outcomes still matter. There is no defensible productivity multiplier from the selected case studies alone. ## 10. What Paradev could productize These are proposed product directions, not a statement that each exists today. 1. **Start from one successful run.** Offer to save its instructions, project, environment and output format as a repeatable workflow. 2. **Suggest a narrow trigger.** Let the user choose assignment, review request or reaction before broader automatic intake. 3. **Keep one task history.** Connect the original signal, sessions, PR, evidence, review and current owner. 4. **Represent verification gaps.** Show which behavior was checked, at which commit and which environment, alongside anything still unverified. 5. **Surface the next decision.** Route attention to blocked work and review queues instead of requiring someone to inspect every tab. 6. **Propose process changes from repeated corrections.** Make them reviewable and versioned, with examples for checking the change. Our Home and Coda workflows supply concrete examples. Your original primitives supply the general model. The onboarding opportunity is helping users build their first useful loop, then making its operation and outcomes visible. ## 11. Suggested talk sequence - Open with a recurring task the audience recognizes. - Recall the production-line framework and show why more coding can increase the review queue. - Walk through a single opt-in triage run. - Show how saved instructions and a trigger make it repeatable. - Use Coda and The Home to demonstrate a more developed chain. - Show where human scope and unverified behavior still require attention. - Close with the improvement loop and what the audience can start with. Possible closing line: “Pick one task you keep doing. Make the next result easier to inspect. Then automate the handoff.” ## Source appendix The following sections preserve the retrieved note bodies as historical source material. They are reference notes, not all proposed talk copy. Their goals, statuses, examples and commands may describe earlier product behavior. The Mastra recording and transcript are linked above. The original editable slide file has not been located. Kiet’s Q3 Product Roadmap Source: Kiet’s Q3 Product Roadmap Location: Company / Archive / Avi’s Q3 Product Roadmap Last edited: # Vision Agents are now there, the bottle neck for a 10-person \$1B company is no longer intelligence, its collecting the techniques and infrastructure required to run a large org with less engineers. We should not build a software factory initially. Instead, we build the building blocks for our users to build the factory. Our first users has always been ourselves and the parts of the product that flop are things we don’t use ourselves: - Linear - Chat GUI - Remote workspaces - CLI (initially)

The question becomes:

What are the building blocks we should create for the factory? ### Building blocks #### 1. Triggers

Trigger is the starting point of the whole process, this can be a schedule, a manual

Example: - Automation - Webhook/trigger - Manual trigger

It should also allow for moving from 1 stage of the factory into the next.

#### 2. Workspace The environment in which the agent + human can do the work, inspection of the work, etc. It could also be used to do verification, review, etc. Example: - Local worktree - Cloud sandbox #### 3. Memory A way to glue the stages and pieces of the factory together and to continuously improve the factory. It can be as simple as docs that the agents at each step can refer to or fancy skills and MCPs #### 4. Visibility No factories can be viable without very good metrics and data to which the factory can be tuned and improved. This can include dashboards, review, tuning

## What’s the end state?

In 12 months, an engineer using Superset uses it like so:

They find out about Superset through people talking about how it 10x their development flow

They onboard to the product and is immediately productive.

It takes an intent they have: “Given my project, I want to ship feature A”.

It allows them to use the best state of the art model for everything.

While it’s shipping, they are prompted once again: “what do you want to do next?” “Given my project, I want to ship feature B”. It goes and does it, prompting them again.

They are able to see both features and their current state, it prompts them when they need to add input, saves or offers to save learnings as it goes. Helping them all the way until the feature is merged.

Once they’re comfortable and have time again, it prompts them to continue doing, or hook up automations like triggers, etc. It then ingests their tasks, give some candidates to scale up.

If they scale too fast it warns them about throughput. They scale up slowly while keeping quality high. They 10x their development. They bring it into their org, each member adds more throughput but still own their own flow. The whole factory gets better over time. Within a few weeks the whole org is shipping 10x more.

What do we ship now?

Working backwards from the vision, we want to get to the final state:
  • Fully functional factory
    • Trigger goes all the way to PR
    • Minimal human interaction, only at important points
    • Good review and inspection
    • Good metrics on the factory and throughput
    • Self-improving given metrics
  • Current state - Manual trigger - Heavy human interaction - No visibility in defect and throughput - No self-improvement - Manual review and inspection
### Goes into buckets: - Trigger - Integrations - Linear + other ticketing - First class Slack + Discord bot support - Automations
  • Needs a lot more work and needs to be a bigger part of the experience
- Review - Agent-driven review - Artifacts and better UI - Visibility - Merge rate - Cost - Dwell time - Policies on how long something dwells - Defect rate - Etc. - Self-improving - Knowledge is stored and iterated on - Can just be markdown files or docs - Workspace - Cloud sandboxes #### How to spend the next 3 months? - Build the primitives - Improve the core part of the business - Cut un-needed parts

Homework (Kiet) 1 Source: 📔 Homework (Kiet) 1 Location: Company / Planning Exercise Last edited: # Purpose The purpose of this exercise is to maximize the quality of our planning discussion. We can document independently before reading anyone else’s responses. We’re not necessarily trying to build a consensus we’re trying to surface the strongest ideas, disagreements, assumptions, opportunities estimated time: 2-3hrs. ---

  • Duplicate this page and add it to the Planning Exercise document
  • Be specific and opinionated
  • Complete independently
  • Try best to separate evidence from assumptions and focus on the ideas you think matter most
--- 1\. Twelve-Month Success

What are the three most important outcomes Superset should achieve over the next 12 months?

Example: Engineering teams move materially faster when using Superset. ### Outcome 1 - Self improving software factory Outcome: Engineering teams can run self-improving software factory with superset Why it matters:

Self-improving because it’s a runaway advantage. Makes it hard to switch from and once you’re in superset your experience keeps getting better.

How we would know it happened: Teams continuously increase PR merge rate while engineers spend constant or less time/interaction per PR --- ### Outcome 2 - The single workspace Outcome: Superset can be used to drive all of an engineer’s work. Including browser and computer use to get anything they need. Why it matters: We don’t want any reason for users to leave the app at all. There’s no structural reason we couldn’t do this either. How we would know it happened:

Users spend more and more of their time in the app and the diversity of work they do in superset changes to include most of their other work. Like triaging, reviewing, CI, etc.

--- ### Outcome 3 - Teams Outcome: Superset becomes the way that teams manage their engineering. Why it matters:

Most serious engineering is done within teams, right now the ecosystem is very fragmented. Teams all need this.

How we would know it happened: We have high saturation within teams and they all use superset as their main driver.

--- 2\. Biggest Opportunities List your 5 highest-leverage ideas. For each opportunity, include: - Description: What would we build or change? - Problem: What problem does it solve? - Customer value: How would it improve the customer’s experience or results? - Company value: How could it improve adoption, retention, revenue, differentiation, or learning? - Outcome supported: Which 12-month outcome does it advance? - Strategic importance: Why is this important to Superset specifically? - Confidence: this will deliver value described: Low, medium, or high - Estimated effort: Small, medium, or large - Risks: What could make this fail or become more expensive than expected?
Opportunity 1 - Software factory Description: Software factory Problem: Writing software is still very manual right now. But not in the right way. Users are typing the same prompt and clicking the same buttons and wasting a lot of time. Customer value: Users save time and become 10x more productive, spending their time where it matters. Company value: Increase adoption Outcome supported: #1, Self improving software factory Strategic importance: It’s the future and mission of the company Confidence: High Estimated effort: Large Risks:

Someone gets there first. Or we’re first but people catch up.

There’s a chance it’s not possible or useful. Users don’t want it. Opportunity 2 - Self improving Description: Self improving loops Problem:

Users learnings aren’t being saved and introspected on, especially across agents. I still manually or tell the agents so save learnings when they should not need me to.

Customer value: Users save time and get better results over time Company value: More adoption Outcome supported: #1, Self improving software factory Strategic importance: Learnings for users can be shared across everyone, creating massive moat Differentiation as no one is doing this Confidence: High Estimated effort: High Risks:

Not being able to do it well. Spend a lot of effort on it just for model labs to do it better.

Opportunity 3 - Single workspace Description: Be the single point of entry for any engineering work Problem: Users still have to leave the platform to review code, check CI, use the browser, etc. Customer value: Users don’t need to context switch for anything Company value: More usage, more engagement Outcome supported: #2 Single workspace you need Strategic importance: Users are more engaged Confidence: Medium Estimated effort: Medium Risks: Scope expansion and lack of ability to achieve it Opportunity 4 - Teams Description: Superset for teams Problem: Engineering with AI between team members is still unsolved and annoying learnings aren’t easily shared between team members Customer value: Teams can all get better together and work better + faster Company value: Huge advantage for teams, easier buy Outcome supported: #3 Teams Strategic importance: It’s harder for a full team to churn, especially when they invest their workflows and processes into superset Confidence: High Estimated effort: High Risks: Diluting the individual users’ performance. Not achieving enough buy-in per team to get value Opportunity 5 - Open orchestrator Description: The truly open orchestrator between agents Problem: Using the app is still manual, users still interact directly with agents. Platform risks for users to use a single provider / agent Customer value:

Customers aren’t locked into 1 solution, less risk. They’re also able to use open models, etc.

Company value: Cost savings, better performance and access to latest and greatest Outcome supported: #2 Single workspace Strategic importance:

It’s how we wouldn’t get squished by the model labs

Confidence: Low Estimated effort: Medium Risks: Still very competitive, there are many small players. Single lab can still dominate and we’d lose because there’s no competition 3\. Rank your proposed opportunities from highest priority to lowest:
1. Software factory
2. Self improving
3. Single workspace
4. Teams
5. Open orchestrator 4\. What we should NOT build now List five ideas that should not be prioritized during the next 12 months. This could include Features, customer segments, integrations 1. All of the integrations 1. Why not now - We should do a small list of most important but it’s not feasible to maintain without large team 2. What could cause us to reconsider - Once we have more engineering efforts or some high value integrations might be worth it 2. Remote workspace 1. Why not now - Not useful enough to enough users, highly complex 2. What could cause us to reconsider - If there’s real large customer demands for self-hosting remote workspaces 3. Real-time 1. Why not now - Not useful enough to enough users, highly complex 2. What could cause us to reconsider - Once real big teams are asking for it For each: - Idea - Why not now - What could cause us to reconsider 5\. Strategic Advantages

List everything you think our durable advantages:

1. Optimized and polished product 2. Lots of money while being very small 3. Got 2 enterprise contracts 4. Well known product in the niche 5. Open source 6. No data yet but we could 7. Speed 6\. Success Metrics List what you think our top 3 success metrics you think we should care about: 1. Revenue 2. DAU 3. Enterprise contracts signed 7\. Reflection Finish these sentences:
  1. The most important strategic bet 1. Self-improving software factory
  2. The top quarterly priority 1. Get there while bringing our users along
  3. I think the team underestimates 1. How quickly we can get there
  4. I think the team overestimates 1. How much work getting a factory locally is
--- The Factory Foundation Source: 🏭 The Factory Foundation Location: Company / Planning Exercise / Sprints Last edited: ## Objective Lay the factory's substrate: machine-unbound cloud workspaces, programmatic control of everything the UI can do, and work flowing in through tickets. ## Scope - [ ] Orchestration Chat - [x] Managed Cloud Experience - [x] Mobile - [x] Usage based Pricing/Token Tracking ## Exit criteria (draft — ratify in planning) - Cloud workspace ready ≤10s from click; sandbox-backed workspaces GA'd - Linear ticket → workspace → PR-with-proof loop live - Full workspace/agent lifecycle drivable via CLI + SDK; an agent can spawn a reviewer subagent - Usage tier live with metering; first usage MRR ## In this cycle - Sandboxes — isolated, machine-unbound environments; replaces the hosts architecture - Shared cloud environments — cloud workspaces as shared team environments - Superset SDK / API — the public integration surface, mirroring the CLI 1:1 - Full headless support through CLI — scripted control; agents spawn agents - Native Tasks System — assign agent work through Linear, report results back - Sandbox permissions — see open decisions - Superset Mobile — see open decisions - Usage-based billing — metering + invoicing; prereq for router take-rate - Cloud backed chat → Stored in cloud - SOP/Artifact/MD files/Processes & Systems → Build in opinions about introspection and self improving → introspect to figure out what processes should be codified → Figure out how to make a recursive loop ## Open decisions - This is two cycles in one. Eight projects (five M/L) spanning cloud infra + mobile + monetization won't fit 4 weeks. Proposal: keep the substrate (Sandboxes, SDK/API, Headless CLI, Native Tasks) and split Monetization (usage billing → token tracking) and Mobile into their own later cycles. - "Orchestration Chat" is in scope here but its project row lives in First Production Line — reconcile. - Sandbox permissions was explicitly "wait for enterprise to ask" — in or out?

# Questions:

  • Figure out what the use case is for web
## Risks - Sandboxes carries the v2 fix-or-pause decision (8 agent-launch users/30d on v2 vs 4,814 on v1) — sequencing risk for everything downstream First Production Line Source: 🏭 First Production Line Location: Company / Planning Exercise / Sprints Last edited: # Focus Run the factory end-to-end for the first time: a trigger fires, work fans out to parallel agents, results come back verified, and a human touches only what needs judgment. # Why now Every prior cycle built a piece — stable base, full workspace, team rails, programmatic substrate, trust layer. This cycle composes them into the thing the mission statement promises, and produces the demo-able story for customers and the Series A narrative. # Exit criteria (draft — proposed, ratify in planning) - One orchestrated task decomposes into ≥3 parallel worktree agents and lands as merged, verified PRs - Automations fire on schedule and events (cron, GitHub PR/release, webhooks) with launch templates live - Median time-to-unblock a waiting agent cut ≥50%; attention routed by queue, not tab-checking # In this cycle - Orchestration chat — one chat plans, fans out, and aggregates parallel agents; the supervisor pattern as a surface. - Automations MVP + event triggers — scheduled and event-triggered agents; flaky-test fixer, Sentry-alert→draft-PR templates. - Attention Queue — running / blocked / waiting-review with needs-input first; push notifications that deep-link to the blocked agent. # Open decisions - What is the flagship "production line" demo story (which trigger, which repo, which proof)? - Does a Monetization cycle (usage billing → model router → cost console) follow immediately after — or displace something earlier, given ARR is the primary KPI? # Out of scope Factory marketplace / social ideas, multi-repo workspaces, eval leaderboards. Video notes Source: Video notes Last edited: # CLI Video Series — 2 videos Video 1 = you drive the CLI (\~3 min). Video 2 = your agent drives it (\~3 min). Demo project: `demo-app` at `~/workplace/demo-app` — planted bug: login redirects to `/dashbord` (typo) → 404. Live IDs: - Project: `e1a9e739-01ec-4068-8dd0-b3fb96b89854` - Workspace `fix-login-bug`: `9c2fa0b2-e746-479f-8e0d-52c57e046fe8` - Claude session: `c9c6b51e-5749-4072-83ec-d6ac3a4ac40c` - Automation: `66598ed3-aae1-48ca-9476-e43c3c9173ea` (paused — resume before filming) --- ## Video 1 — The Superset CLI ### 1. Cold open Usually you can use the superset app from the app UI. But you can drive it all from the terminal using our CLI. Here’s a single command to create a new workspace, and spin up claude code to fix a bug

Then: "One command. Isolated workspace, agent already working on the bug." ```bash superset workspaces create \ --project e1a9e739-01ec-4068-8dd0-b3fb96b89854 \ --name "fix-login-bug" \ --branch fix/login-bug \ --local \ --agent claude \ --prompt "Signing in lands on a 404. Fix the login redirect bug and add a regression test." ``` Show: the bug first — `npm start`, Sign in, 404. Then run it. Hard cut. ### 2. Setup — once, 30 seconds Say: "Install, sign in, done." ```bash brew install superset-sh/tap/superset superset auth login ``` ### 3. Point it at your repo Say: "Use the checkout you already have." ```bash superset projects create --name "demo-app" --local --import ~/workplace/demo-app ``` ### 4. The one command, explained Say: "Own branch, own worktree — your checkout is untouched. And it's all in the app." ```bash superset workspaces open 9c2fa0b2-e746-479f-8e0d-52c57e046fe8 ``` Show: desktop app opens on the workspace, Claude working in the pane. ### 5. Steer from any terminal Say: "Glance at it. Redirect it.
